name: Lemon juice on pimples

lead: Some people apply lemon juice to pimples and dark marks, citing its citric acid and vitamin C, hoping to dry spots out and fade marks for a clearer, more even look.
Lemon juice is about 5-6% citric acid and a rich source of vitamin C, and believers credit these for the effect. No clinical studies of lemon juice for acne were found.

paras: Fresh juice is dabbed onto individual blemishes or marks, typically as a home remedy, and sometimes diluted.
Citrus juice on skin followed by sun exposure can cause phytophotodermatitis, with blistering and pigmentation that can last years.

chain: Acid and vitamin C on blemish
angle.text: Lemon juice is dabbed on pimples and dark marks in the belief that its acid and vitamin C dry spots out and fade marks for more even skin. This is a home-remedy tradition, and no studies were found on it for acne.

lead: Dabbing lemon juice on pimples is a home remedy people use to dry out blemishes and fade the marks they leave, aiming for clearer, more even skin. Proponents point to lemon juice's citric acid and vitamin C, saying the acidity dries excess oil and the vitamin C calms redness.[1]

Lemon juice is about 5 to 6 percent citric acid and a rich source of vitamin C, according to Wikipedia.[2] Healthline reports that the claimed benefits (reducing oil, killing acne-linked bacteria, easing redness and leftover scars) come mostly from online forums and blogs, and that vitamin C has been studied for acne less than zinc or retinoids.[1]

Dermatology-oriented coverage lists the documented downsides of applying citrus juice to the skin: dryness, stinging, redness, increased sun sensitivity and possible hyperpigmentation, and Wikipedia describes phytophotodermatitis, a reaction to plant compounds plus UVA light that can leave pigment marks for years.[1][3] No clinical study of lemon juice itself for acne was found.
infobox: Fewer, less red blemishes; fading of marks

paras: Healthline summarises what proponents say: citric acid dries out sebum, the juice kills acne-associated bacteria such as P. acnes, and its vitamin C eases inflammation and redness, including in post-acne marks.[1] The same article says such claims are mostly anecdotal and found in forums and blogs.[1]
Wikipedia reports lemon juice contains roughly 5 to 6 percent citric acid and is a rich source of vitamin C.[2]

Healthline notes that vitamin C has been studied for acne less extensively than zinc or vitamin A (retinoids), and that there is no scientific proof for lemon juice fading acne scars; chemical peels and dermabrasion have more research behind them.[1]
No studies found of lemon juice applied to pimples.

Healthline lists sun sensitivity, dryness, burning, stinging, itching and redness, and says citrus may cause hyperpigmentation, particularly a concern for darker skin tones.[1] Phytophotodermatitis follows contact with light-sensitising plant compounds (furanocoumarins) and UVA exposure; redness and burning appear within 24 hours, blisters can form within 48 hours, and brown or purplish discolouration can last for years.[3] Wikipedia's article names lime juice as its example and does not specifically mention lemon.[3]

lore.intro: Lemon juice appears in home-remedy discussions of acne as a spot treatment.[1]

claims.claim: Lemon juice on skin plus sunlight can cause lasting discolouration
